rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The treaty dispute became urgent during the sūra’s revelation because many women migrated to Madīnah, making a definite Muslim policy necessary.
rows.anchor: many women also migrated to Madī nah and it became essential that Muslims adopt a definite policy in this regard.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims must assess whether migrant women came for Islam; they may not return true believers, while retaining women who came for other reasons is also unlawful because Islamic society is for the pious.
rows.anchor: their faith must be assessed and evaluated, and without this process, they must not be accepted in their community

rows.speaker: Ibn ‘Abbās
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the Prophet tested women’s motives by oaths: they had not come from marital resentment, desire to move, or worldly motives, but from love of God and His Prophet.
rows.anchor: Ibn ‘Abbā s was asked: “How did the Prophet (sws) assess women?” He answered: “He would ask them to swear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase that God knows their faith is parenthetical: Muslims should assess women by oaths and other means, while recognizing that God alone knows their reality.
rows.anchor: Muslims should try to asses these women by taking oaths from them and by other

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God fully knows their true faith; Muslims are excused if diligent assessment cannot uncover it, while deceptive women should know God knows the extent of their faith or its absence.
rows.anchor: If, in spite of trying, Muslims are not able to get to the truth in this matter, then they have a legitimate excuse before God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If available assessment proves the migrants are believers, they must not be returned because the believing women and disbelieving husbands are unlawful to one another.
rows.anchor: if through available means of assessment, it is proved that they are believing women, then they must not be returned to the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an resolved the Ḥudaybiyyah treaty dispute fairly: it required return of women who migrated for worldly reasons but protected those proven to be believers, rather than exploiting treaty wording alone.
rows.anchor: With this directive, the Qur’ān, once and for all, decided the dispute which had arisen about a statute of the treaty of Ḥudaybiyyah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ruling protects a person’s moral and intellectual identity from an unsafe society; women deserve special protection because they are the weaker gender.
rows.anchor: especially women, being the weaker gender, deserve even more to be protected.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims must reimburse the former husband’s dower for a detained believing woman; the public treasury should fund it, and the general wording implies dower by the context of separation.
rows.anchor: it is the responsibility of the Muslims to pay back to her husband the dower he had paid her.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After these steps, a Muslim may marry the woman by reimbursing her former husband’s dower and paying her a new dower.
rows.anchor: pay back the dower paid by the former husband and then to pay a fresh dower

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Her disbelieving husband or relatives cannot prevent the marriage or require their permission; she is free to choose within the limits of sharīʿah.
rows.anchor: She is now free of the restraints of her disbelieving husband and relatives, and can exercise her free will within the limits of the sharī‘ah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ʿiṣam is the plural of ʿiṣmah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islam took a generous, one-sided step by directing Muslims to release disbelieving wives living in the abode of disbelief so they could marry whom they wished.
rows.anchor: Muslims were directed to release from wedlock their wives, who were disbelievers and were living in the dār al-kufr.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once the marriages ended, dowers were to be exchanged reciprocally: each side returned the dower paid by its husbands to the wives who had left.
rows.anchor: As far as their dowers were concerned, they should be mutually exchanged.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an rejected Quraysh’s demand that the treaty required returning Muslim women; its just, comprehensive verdict solved a social dilemma and closed the way to further dispute, so believers should trust God’s wisdom.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ ān did not accept the demand of the Quraysh that as per the terms of the treaty, it was mandatory on the Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word means “then came your turn” or “you were given the opportunity.”
rows.anchor: or you were given the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If disbelievers violate the dower-exchange procedure and withhold a dower owed to a Muslim husband, Muslims may pay that Muslim from funds otherwise owed to the disbelievers; this fair retaliation is allowed because one party acted unjustly.
rows.anchor: by the Qur’ān and was allowed by it because one of the parties was being unjust.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even when using this retaliatory permission, Muslims must fear God, avoid seeking unjustified excuses, and take no more than their due.
rows.anchor: Muslims should fear God in whom they have professed faith even while dealing with their enemies.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Women coming to join the Muslims should pledge to obey Islam’s good commands and avoid sins common in jāhiliyyah, preventing those practices from spreading in the Muslim community.
rows.anchor: A pledge should be sought from them to obey all the good enjoined by Islam and to promise to specially refrain

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the time, women were pledging Islam in large numbers, including many from morally degraded jāhiliyyah groups; they needed to learn the new society’s standards and enter intending to change.
rows.anchor: many of these women belonged to the morally decrepit sections of the society in the time of jāhiliyyah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first pledge is to avoid associating partners with God: pure monotheism is the foundation of religion and begins by renouncing polytheism; without that understanding, people may claim monotheism while practicing shirk.
rows.anchor: The foundation of the whole religion is the pure belief of monotheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition on theft means that violating human rights is as wrong as violating God’s rights.
rows.anchor: it is equally wrong and forbidden to infringe upon the rights of human beings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third pledge is that women should not commit adultery.
rows.anchor: The third of these directives is that they should not commit adultery:
